source.title: THE DIFFUSE LIGHT OF THE UNIVERSE: On the microwave background before and after its discovery: open questions

accepted.question_text: Is the cosmic microwave background necessarily of cosmological origin and inseparable from the big bang, or can the same sky-filling microwave radiation be explained within other cosmological theories or by other physical mechanisms? Here, the cosmological interpretation is the claim that the observed background is fossil light released in an early hot, dense universe; the competing possibility is that the observed microwave background could arise through non-big-bang mechanisms while still accounting for the measured diffuse radiation.

evidence.quote: This is an important weakness of the present consensus cosmological model that justifies raising several questions on the CMB interpretation. Can we consider its cosmological nature as undisputable? Do other possible interpretations exist in the context of other cosmological theories or simply as a result of other physical mechanisms that could account for it?
So, is it really inseparable from the big bang? Can the same radiation be interpreted differently by other mechanisms and cosmological theories?
Considering these different works, can we really consider the diffuse microwave radiation as an "indisputable" proof of the big bang?

accepted.question_text: At what distance, and with what spatial distribution of sources, is the observed 3 K microwave background actually produced? More specifically, is it only a very distant fossil background emitted in the early universe, or could it instead be a more universal radiation field produced partly or wholly locally and at long distances, given that its smooth blackbody spectrum does not itself provide a direct distance measurement?
accepted.context_brief: Distance and locality of the 3K radiation

evidence.quote: No direct distance measurement can therefore be performed. At a consequence, this radiation could actually be produced - for all or part - in any region of the universe.

The nature of diffuse radiation is therefore a much more open question than it seems a priori. Is it really only a very distant fossil background radiation or simply a more universal radiation, filling the entire space and produced both locally and at long distances?

accepted.question_text: Can observations decisively establish whether the 3 K microwave background comes from a very early epoch by directly verifying predicted signatures of a primordial origin, such as a higher background temperature at larger redshift or spectral distortions that reveal the production redshift near recombination around z≈1000? This remains open because current indirect temperature probes using CN, carbon, and CO excitation can be contaminated by other processes, and the proposed recombination-era spectral test may be too weak for present or near-future instruments.

evidence.quote: Even after the recent results of the Planck satellite, there is still a pending fundamental question about the 3K radiation: is it, yes or no, a distant background radiation, coming from a very early period in time?

We should be able, for example, to measure the temperature of the microwave radiation at different redshifts that is in regions more and more distant in the universe. We would then be able to check if, as predicted by the big bang, the further back we are in the past, the higher is the temperature.
So these single results are still far from delivering the expected definitive proof. There is therefore no fully reliable thermometer of cosmic microwave radiation today.
A much more ambitious test would be to measure the redshift at the exact time when the 3K was produced that is to say at a redshift of approximately 1000.
